Your Images, in Your Hands

Sharing whole imaging studies with a SMART Health Link

One link can carry a complete imaging study: every DICOM file, pixels unchanged, end-to-end encrypted on a host that never holds the key. Any app that can fetch and decrypt can open it.

Josh Mandel · shlink-dicom · October 2026

Open the sample
shlink-dicom.exe.xyz/sample

The question

Patients have a legal right to copies of their imaging. In practice a study usually arrives on a CD, or can be looked at in a provider's portal.

SMART Health Links share health records by link or QR code: a URL to an encrypted file plus the key to open it.

SMART Imaging Access lets patients use any app they choose to fetch imaging from their providers through standard APIs (FHIR and DICOMweb).

Can one link carry a whole study, every DICOM file, in a form any app can fetch?

Trust and lifecycle

Sharer's deviceReads the files, can compress them losslessly, encrypts each study under its own key. Sees the study.
HostStores bundle.jwe and one encrypted file per study. Sees random file names, sizes and byte ranges; no names, UIDs or keys.
Recipient's deviceOpens the link, checks every record, decrypts, decodes. Sees the study.

Plaintext exists only on the two devices. The key travels in the link, after the #.

  • Owner link. No accounts. The owner page shows how often each link was opened, and revokes it: then the server answers 404.
  • Re-share a subset without re-uploading. Each study has its own key, so a link to one study is just a new bundle.jwe holding that study's key.
  • Storage. Local disk, or a private S3 bucket. Reads go through the server by default; in redirect mode the presigned URLs last 60 seconds at most.

Standards work

  • Pull request #5 to argonautproject/smart-imaging (open): transfer-syntax negotiation for WADO-RS.
  • Issue #2 (open): the token response example omits token_type and scope.
  • Issue #3 (open): what apps send for transfer syntax, and what happens when it is omitted.
  • Building a strict server and client against the guide found 14 places where it was unclear.
  • The profile and its extensions use URLs under the HL7 SMART Health Cards and Links guide, proposed for publication there.

One slice, from link to pixels

Traced by script on the live sample, 16 Oct 2026, 04:19 CDT: brain MRI, series 16, instance 11. The share: 6 encrypted files, one per study, 313.4 MB.

Clients that can follow the same link

The link and files are plain HTTP, FHIR and DICOM. Any program that can fetch, check and decrypt can use them.

built: /viewBrowser viewerFetches only the records for the images on screen, one Range request each.
built: receiver.jsDownload scriptAbout 60 lines of fetch and WebCrypto: resolve the link, decrypt the Bundle, read and check records.
possible, not built herePACS importFetch each study file whole, check every tag, write the original DICOM files into the archive.
possible, not built hereResearch pipelineRead the Bundle's index, fetch just the series it needs, and decode them with its own tools.

What it does

Viewer

  • CT and MR reformats: oblique planes, slabs
  • X-rays with their VOI LUTs
  • Whole-slide pathology, tile by tile
  • Video, including MPEG-2
  • Structured reports (dose)
  • Segmentations
  • Encapsulated PDF
  • Reports beside the images
  • Download: a ZIP with DICOMDIR
  • Dark mode
  • Phone layout

Sharing

  • Files, a folder, a CD, an archive
  • From a link someone sent
  • From a provider, by SMART Imaging Access
  • Lossless JPEG or JPEG 2000
  • Resumable uploads
  • Local disk or S3 storage
  • Owner link: open counts, revoke

Evidence from real files

Decoders, against reference decoders

1,000 / 1,000random IDC files decoded exactly as the references do (95% interval 99.62–100%)
9,522 / 9,537IDC files picked for rare scanners, software and encodings passed. The 15 others: 8 lack Planar Configuration (now inferred), 4 Leica JPEG 2000 off by ≤3 (ruled acceptable), 3 float maps (now decoded).
832real-image cases in the decoder test corpus, all passing
867 / 885renderings of real files on which dcmtk agrees within one grey level. The 18 others: 7 from our VOI LUT bit-depth rule, 8 with no stored window, 2 off by two levels, 1 where pydicom sides with us.

JPEG 2000 and HTJ2K results re-checked with the new decoder: corpus byte-identical; 185 IDC long-tail JPEG 2000 files with the same outcome.

Lossless encoders

2.46×smaller with lossless JPEG (SV1) on Josh's five studies, 403 → 164 MB. Every image decodes bit-exact in libjpeg, GDCM and dcmtk.
2.96×with lossless JPEG 2000, 403 → 136 MB; bit-exact under three OpenJPEG-based decoders.

Scripted browser checks

Live: How it works 254 / 255 (one task took 109 ms; the limit is 100) · sandbox 153 / 153.

Object types, viewed end to end

120 / 156cases pass, across 43 object types: all in IDC, plus five it lacks. 22 fail, from seven defects being fixed; 14 are labelled not displayed, with a download.

IDC has no Enhanced or Legacy Converted CT, MR or PET; those came from public test files and series derived from IDC.

Questions that removed design layers

“What's the zip buying us?”

No ZIP container: offsets in the ImagingStudy and the GCM tags already locate and protect every byte.

“I don't love optionality here, how does a client even know what's deflated.”

No optional compression layer: DICOM already carries its own compression, so every client has one code path.

“Final record delimiter… why is that needed? Doesn't ending at that point also accomplish the same?”

No end-of-file marker: the Bundle states every length, so a cut-short file shows up in the arithmetic.

“Why use HKDF at that point?”

No key derivation: each file has its own random key, carried in the Bundle.
